content.text:
# Capture Instrument

A thin Chrome extension paired with a local server to save X/Twitter posts
(text + links + curated comments) you care about, add notes, and keep them
durably. While a capture is pending you can ask a **local pi agent** (the
capture agent service) to reason over it — summarise, find the core claim,
fetch and read the urls inside it — and on Save the capture persists with an
`agent` envelope linking the full conversation as evidence. Saved captures are
searchable through a derived SQLite FTS5 index exposed by the server.

See `docs/vision/VISION.md` for the product vision. The PRD that drives this
implementation lives in the workspace under
`docs/prd-queue/2026-08-08-extension-inline-agent.md`.

## Layout

```
capture/
├── extension/       # Chrome MV3 extension (unpacked, Brave/Chromium)
│   ├── manifest.json
│   ├── content.js     # on x.com: single Capture pill (hover), recursive node scraper,
│   │                  #   open-capture state (root + curated comments), on-page highlight
│   ├── sidepanel.html # panel UI: live tree view + notes + Ask (agent) + Save
│   ├── sidepanel.js   # render the recursive tree, gather notes, ask/follow-up/abort the
│   │                  #   agent, stamp the agent envelope, POST the tree to server
│   ├── agent-client.js# thin WebSocket client for the agent service (reconnect/backoff)
│   └── background.js  # service worker: keeps capture state across navigation
├── agent-service/   # local Node + pi SDK reasoning service (ws://127.0.0.1:8766)
│   ├── server.js      # WebSocket routes ask / follow_up / abort; persists evidence
│   ├── agent.js       # createAgentSession (in-memory, tools=[fetch_url]), streams events
│   ├── serialize.js   # capture tree -> text injected into the first prompt
│   ├── persist.js     # write sessions/<uuid>/session.jsonl (pi-native v3) + envelope
│   ├── models.mjs     # OpenRouter model stack (deepseek/deepseek-v4-flash, key from env)
│   └── tools/fetch_url.js # the one custom tool (size/time caps; server-side fetch)
└── server/          # local FastAPI server
    ├── server.py          # POST /api/capture (validates tree + agent envelope) -> data/artefacts.jsonl
    │                      # GET  /search (read API over the FTS5 index)
    ├── index.py           # SQLite + FTS5 (BM25) schema + insert/query helpers
    ├── bin/rebuild-index.py # rebuild data/index.db from data/artefacts.jsonl
    ├── data/              # artefacts.jsonl, sessions/<uuid>/session.jsonl, index.db (all gitignored)
    ├── requirements.txt
    └── tests/test_capture.py
```

## Architecture

```
User on x.com (detail page) → hover tweet → Capture pill (root)
    → content.js scrapes root node, side panel opens, capture stays in progress
    → comments below show the same pill; click to add (nested by DOM parent) / remove
    → sidepanel.js shows the live indented tree
    → [optional] Ask → agent-service reasons over the tree + urls (fetch_url),
      streams the answer; on settle returns { sessionId, sessionFile, model, cost }
    → sidepanel.js stashes the agent envelope on the pending capture
    → Save → POST /api/capture { root node with nested children, maybe { agent } }
    → server.py validates recursively + envelope, stamps captured_at, appends a line
      to data/artefacts.jsonl, and the agent service has already written the full
      conversation to data/sessions/<uuid>/session.jsonl (evidence)
    → bin/rebuild-index.py derives data/index.db (FTS5) → GET /search?q=… → ranked
      results, each linking to its session evidence
```

## Running

### Capture server (Python, port 8765)

```bash
cd capture/server
python -m venv .venv && .venv/bin/pip install -r requirements.txt   # once
.venv/bin/python -m uvicorn server:app --host 127.0.0.1 --port 8765
```

Defaults: `127.0.0.1:8765`, data at `capture/server/data/artefacts.jsonl`.
Each is overridable by one env var (`CAPTURE_PORT`, `CAPTURE_DATA`,
`CAPTURE_INDEX`). No config file, no CLI flags.

### Agent service (Node, port 8766) — optional but powers Ask

```bash
cd capture/agent-service
npm install
OPENROUTER_API_KEY=… node server.js        # ws://127.0.0.1:8766
```

The key lives only in the service's environment — never in the browser. If
it is not set, or the service is not running, the side panel shows an
"agent unavailable" state and saving still works exactly as before.

> **Note:** a running server does not pick up changes to `server.py`. If you
> edit the server, **restart it**. If the extension saves but the JSONL doesn't
> reflect new fields, a stale server process is the usual cause.

Test the capture endpoint directly:

```bash
curl -X POST http://127.0.0.1:8765/api/capture \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"tweet_url":"https://x.com/user/status/123","tweet_text":"hello","notes":"n"}'
```

Test search (rebuild the index first, or let /search build it on first use):

```bash
cd capture/server && .venv/bin/python bin/rebuild-index.py --verbose
curl "http://127.0.0.1:8765/search?q=arxiv"
```

## Loading the extension (Brave / Chrome)

1. Open `brave://extensions` (or `chrome://extensions`).
2. Enable **Developer mode**.
3. **Load unpacked** → select `capture/extension/`.
4. Navigate to x.com. On a tweet's page, hover a tweet → the **Capture** pill
   appears; click it to start a capture (the side panel opens and stays open).
   Scroll the comments — each shows the same pill; click to add it (it nests
   under its parent and is highlighted on the page), click again to remove.
   Add notes and click **Save**.

If the server isn't running when you Save, the panel shows **"Server offline —
restart and try again"** and keeps your data so you can retry after starting it.
If the agent service isn't running (or OpenRouter is unavailable), the **Ask**
panel shows "agent unavailable" and Save still works.

## API contract

- `POST /api/capture`
  - Body: a **recursive node tree** — the root tweet with optional `children`
    (curated comments, which may themselves have `children`), plus an optional
    root-level `agent` envelope:
    ```json
    {
      "tweet_url": "https://x.com/user/status/123456",
      "author": "@user",
      "tweet_text": "…",
      "links": ["https://github.com/owner/repo"],
      "parent_url": null,
      "notes": "…",
      "children": [ … ],
      "agent": {
        "sessionId": "<uuid>",
        "sessionFile": "sessions/<uuid>/session.jsonl",
        "prompt": "…",
        "model": "deepseek/deepseek-v4-flash",
        "capturedAt": "…",
        "cost": 0.042
      }
    }
    ```
  - Every node needs `tweet_url` (the anchor); the rest may be empty. The
    server validates **recursively** — every nested `children` node must have
    a `tweet_url`.
  - Each node's `links` mixes external URLs (resolved out of `t.co`) and
    embedded/quote tweet status URLs. A node's own URL is its anchor, never
    duplicated into its links.
  - When `agent` is present it must carry `sessionId` + `sessionFile`
    (`400` otherwise). The server does **not** verify the session file exists
    at save time — session persistence is the agent service's contract.
  - Success: `200` + `{ "status": "saved", "captured_at": "…" }`
  - Invalid/missing required field: `400`
- `captured_at` is stamped by the **server** on the root on receipt.

- `GET /search` (read API over the derived index)
  - Params: `q` (keyword query; supports AND/OR/NOT, phrases, `author:`
    qualifiers, prefix `*`), `author` (exact author filter), `since` (ISO
    timestamp), `limit` (default 50).
  - Returns `{ "items": [ { id, tweet_url, author, tweet_text, links,
    timestamp, agent } ], "total": n, "rank": true }`, relevance-ranked by
    FTS5 BM25.
  - The index is derived from `data/artefacts.jsonl` by
    `bin/rebuild-index.py` (or built on first `/search` if missing).

## Testing

```bash
cd capture/server && .venv/bin/python -m pytest tests/ -q
cd capture/agent-service && AGENT_MOCK=1 npm run smoke   # protocol smoke (no key needed)
```

Manual extension verification: load unpacked, capture a tweet, ask the agent
(stream), Save, confirm the artefact line lands in `data/artefacts.jsonl` with
the `agent` envelope and `data/sessions/<uuid>/session.jsonl` exists, then
search it with `/search`. Personal tool — no automated browser tests.

## Scope

- **Text-only.** Images/screenshots/binary are explicitly out of scope for v1.
- Manual capture only. No auto-capture. No engagement (like/reply/retweet).
- Single user, single machine. Chrome (Brave) only, loaded unpacked.
- The captured data is immutable; downstream apps read and process it.
- Agent evidence (session.jsonl) is saved verbatim and never edited.
- No browser control by the agent (deferred to a follow-on phase).

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Start the Capture local server.
#
# Usage:
#   ./run-server.sh            # start server on 127.0.0.1:8765 (foreground)
#   CAPTURE_PORT=9000 ./run-server.sh
#
# Optional env vars:
#   CAPTURE_PORT   port override (default 8765)
#   CAPTURE_DATA   data file override (default server/data/artefacts.jsonl)
set -euo pipefail

SCRIPT_DIR="$(cd "$(dirname "${BASH_SOURCE[0]}")" && pwd)"
SERVER_DIR="$SCRIPT_DIR/server"
VENV="$SERVER_DIR/.venv"

# Create + install deps on first run (idempotent after).
if [ ! -x "$VENV/bin/python" ]; then
  echo ">> Creating virtualenv at $VENV"
  python3 -m venv "$VENV"
fi

if ! "$VENV/bin/python" -c "import fastapi, uvicorn" 2>/dev/null; then
  echo ">> Installing server dependencies..."
  "$VENV/bin/pip" install -q -r "$SERVER_DIR/requirements.txt"
fi

PORT="${CAPTURE_PORT:-8765}"

echo ">> Starting Capture server on http://127.0.0.1:$PORT"
echo ">> Data file: ${CAPTURE_DATA:-$SERVER_DIR/data/artefacts.jsonl}  (press Ctrl+C to stop)"
cd "$SERVER_DIR"
exec "$VENV/bin/python" -m uvicorn server:app --host 127.0.0.1 --port "$PORT"

The runs for a single operation are collected into a trace . You can link together traces from multi-turn sessions as a thread . A trajectory is another way to structure and visualize that data. While a thread groups the traces of a session and keeps their nested structure, a trajectory flattens the entire session into an ordered list of messages that shows the path an agent took from start to finish. ​ Runs A run represents a single unit of work executed by an agent, such as calling an LLM, formatting a prompt, or retrieving documents. If you are familiar with OpenTelemetry , you can think of a run as a span. ​ Traces A trace is a collection of runs for a single operation. For example, if a user request triggers an agent that calls a model, runs a tool, and then calls the model again, all of those runs belong to the same trace. Runs are bound to a trace by a unique trace ID. Each trace is limited to a maximum of 25,000 runs. Once the trace reaches this limit, LangSmith will reject any additional runs that you send for that trace. ​ Threads A thread is a sequence of traces representing a single multi-turn session. A turn is one exchange in that session: a user’s message and everything the agent does in response. Each turn is recorded as its own trace. To group traces into a thread, pass a thread_id metadata key with a unique value. Learn how to configure threads . ​ Trajectories A trajectory is a flat, ordered list of messages that shows the path an agent took from start to finish. In LangSmith, a trajectory is a projection over the traces in a thread. It contains the human, AI, and tool messages exchanged during the session, each appearing once, in the order it first appeared, with the nesting of runs removed. The Messages view , which renders trajectories in the LangSmith UI, is in beta . Learn how trajectories render in the Messages view . ​ Compare traces, threads, and trajectories Trace Thread Trajectory Shape Tree of runs Sequence of traces Flat, ordered list of messages Contains Every run, with full inputs and outputs Every run in every linked trace Every message in every linked trace, deduplicated Reach for it when You are debugging why one operation failed or ran slow You are inspecting how the agent behaved across turns, with timing and nesting intact You are reading what was exchanged in the session, without the execution detail Use Chat to analyze traces, runs, and threads. Log traces to a project . ​ Trace enrichment ​ Feedback Feedback allows you to score an individual run based on certain criteria. Each feedback entry consists of a tag and a score, and is bound to a run by a unique run ID. Feedback can be continuous or discrete (categorical), and tags can be reused across runs within an organization. For more on how feedback is stored, refer to the Feedback data format guide . ​ Tags Tags are strings you can attach to runs to categorize, filter, and group them in the LangSmith UI. Learn how to attach tags to your traces . ​ Metadata Metadata is a collection of key-value pairs you can attach to runs. # Save Knowledge

## Summary

Read the current session, infer a title for the decision, append it as a new structured entry under `docs/knowledge/sessions/<uuid>/decisions/`, and add a link to `docs/knowledge/index.md`. Multiple decisions from the same session accumulate in the same session directory — each independently addressable in the index.

## Finding the current session

Run this to find the session file:
```bash
ls -t ~/.pi/agent/sessions/--*--/*.jsonl 2>/dev/null | head -1
```
This picks the most recently modified `.jsonl` across all session directories — it's the one being written to right now. Verify by reading the first line (the session header) and confirming it has a `"type":"session"` field.

## Re-running on the same session

Multiple saves from the same session add new decision files to the same session directory. The session directory is keyed by UUID, so subsequent saves always find it. Each decision gets its own sequence number — no overwrites.

## Workflow

1. **Find the current session file** using the command above. Read the first line to get the session UUID.

2. **Create or reuse the session directory**:
   ```
   docs/knowledge/sessions/<uuid>/
   ```
   Create it if it doesn't exist. Then **always copy** the session file into it as `session.jsonl`, overwriting any previous copy. The session file grows as the conversation progresses — each save gets the freshest snapshot, which is a strict superset of any earlier one.

3. **Read the session entries** — the file is JSONL. Walk the tree from leaf to root via `parentId` to get the active path. Skip entries that are excluded by compaction (a compaction entry with `firstKeptEntryId` replaces everything before that point).

4. **Infer a title** from the conversation. The title should be short and descriptive (e.g. "Payment Flow Architecture Decision"). Also derive a slug from the title for the filename.

5. **Determine the next sequence number** — list files in `docs/knowledge/sessions/<uuid>/decisions/`. If the directory doesn't exist yet, start at `01`. Otherwise, find the highest existing numeric prefix and increment by one.

6. **Determine the task slug** — if the session is associated with a task (i.e., the agent is working on a task from `docs/tasks.txt`), look up the task slug from the task file or from the session context. The slug is the `<slug>` portion of the task file path. Include it in the `Task:` field.

7. **Determine the project slug** — derive the project slug from the task's `**Project**:` field (if a task is associated) or from the session context (which project this session relates to). Use the same hyphenated convention as task files (e.g. `survival-infrastructure`, `software-factory`, `workspace-portability`). Include it in the `Project:` field.

8. **Capture the decision** — write a new file at:
   ```
   docs/knowledge/sessions/<uuid>/decisions/<sequence>-<slug>.md
   ```
   Use the structured format below. Every field matters. The **revision triggers** field is especially important — it tells a future agent when to stop trusting this entry.

9. **Append to `docs/knowledge/index.md`** — add a project-grouped entry. The index is organized by project so entries are discoverable by project context. Add:
   ```markdown
   ### <project-slug>
   - [<title>](sessions/<uuid>/decisions/<sequence>-<slug>.md)
   ```
   If the project section already exists, just add the line under it. Create `index.md` with a `# Knowledge Base` heading if it doesn't exist.

## Structured format

```markdown
## Decision: <title>

**Status**: proposed | accepted | deprecated | superseded
**Date**: <yyyy-mm-dd HH:MM>
**Task**: <slug>
**Project**: <slug>
**Session**: sessions/<uuid>/session.jsonl

### Context

What was happening in the workspace that framed this decision.

### Problem

The specific tension or requirement being addressed.

### Alternatives

What else was considered and why each was rejected or deferred.

### Decision

What was chosen.

### Rationale

Why this path, acknowledging trade-offs.

### Consequences

What changes — things that become easier, harder, or deprecated.

### Revision triggers

Conditions that would make this decision worth re-examining.
```

### Context

The product/architecture layer of the software factory had a single phase: grill → PRD → capture decisions. The wsff.md article ("Why Software Factories Fail") proposed a 4-phase planning model — Product Design → System Architecture → Program Design → Vertical Slices — and argued that front-loading alignment reduces rework and review time when working with AI coding agents.

### Problem

The existing product layer produced a PRD and then handed off to the assembly line without intermediate structural analysis.
